toc.title: Why it works: the safety state

blocks.p: Have you ever felt overwhelmed by your emotions? Do you sometimes struggle to understand why you feel or think a certain way? If so, you're not alone. It's easy to get caught up in our thoughts and emotions, and that makes it hard to process our feelings effectively. So let's look at mindfulness, and how it can help with emotional processing.

I know, I know. You're probably tired of hearing about mindfulness. It's everywhere. But hear me out. I think I can make it more practical and understandable, and not so woo-woo. I want you to have greater emotional wellbeing and more self-regulation. I want you to have a strong vagal brake and more resilience to life's challenges. Being able to feel your feelings and improve your emotional processing with mindfulness can really help with that.

Briefly, mindfulness is an experience, I would call it, of non-judgmental awareness that focuses specifically on the present moment. It involves paying attention to your thoughts, emotions, impulses, or bodily sensations, maybe one of them or all of them, without getting sucked into despair or crisis, or being triggered. If you're curious and connected to the present moment, you're being mindful. That's really it.

That awareness of the present moment can come through the external environment: the things around you, being connected to your surroundings. Or it can come through your internal experience, through interoception: being able to look inward and feel what's going on inside.

Mindfulness can be done while moving. It can be done while being still. There's no one right way to be mindful. I think it's actually pretty straightforward conceptually. Are you connected to the present moment in some capacity, internally or externally, through your senses? Or not?

Emotional processing is the ability to feel your difficult feelings and then allow them to reduce in intensity. When that happens, the calming lets you experience more of what the present moment has to offer.

For the polyvagal nerds, I would just call this self-regulation. It's the ability to allow a defensive state, its emotions, sensations, impulses, or cognitions, and to experience them and let them soften.

Mindfulness and emotional processing have a mutually supportive relationship. By practicing mindfulness, you become more aware of your emotions. As you practice being in the present moment and in connection with yourself, then when more difficult emotions come up, you're better able to recognize them, and maybe even welcome them or be with them. That's instead of avoiding them through some coping skill, a numbing-out behavior, or some reflexive behavior. So being more mindful actually makes you better at processing your emotions.

blocks.h: Why it works: the safety state

blocks.p: To understand how mindfulness leads to emotional processing, we need a quick look at what the Polyvagal Theory, from Dr. Stephen Porges, teaches us about the safety state.

When you're connected to the present moment, that's a pretty good indication that your brainstem pathways for safety and social engagement are active. These ventral vagal pathways are responsible for your ability to connect with yourself, with others, and with your external environment. I think the impulse of the safety state is connection.

When these pathways are active, they keep your heartbeat at a calmer pace. That's called the vagal brake, but don't worry about that right now. Keeping your heartbeat calmer keeps your defensive biological pathways from activating. Your flight, fight, and shutdown pathways don't take over, or if they do activate, they don't dominate.

If your body isn't in a defensive state, you won't experience anxiety, anger, panic, and a whole bunch of other, quote-unquote, "negative emotions" that are obstacles to being mindful. In other words, when your body is prepared for safety, you won't be living in those negative emotions. And then you're much more capable of emotional processing. The more negative experiences calm down, and that opens up the possibility for other experiences to surface, possibly safety state ones.

Likewise, if your body is prepared for safety, it's much more able to process your defensive state emotions. If anger surfaces, for example, you'll be able to notice it, allow it, and maybe even mindfully experience it. That process reduces the intensity of the anger.
Practicing mindfulness has to be practical and accessible for you. Here are five techniques that can help you feel your feelings:

ol: Use cognitions to open up the potential for mindfulness: validation, normalization, and permission.
Body scanning, to identify where your emotion lives.

blocks.p: There are three thoughts I want you to give yourself. They help open up the possibility for mindfulness, for being in your safety state, and for emotional processing to happen.

ul: Validation. Is your emotion real? Is what you're going through real? It's kind of like confirmation. You're not evaluating it, not rejecting it, not even really embracing it. You're just asking, objectively, "Is this what I'm feeling?"
Normalization. Does this emotion make sense? Does it make sense based on the context I'm feeling it in? And does it make sense based on the context of my overall life?
Permission. If your emotion is valid and normal, then you can give it permission to exist within your body in the present moment. It's already there anyway, so you might as well give it permission.

blocks.p: After those brain-to-body messages, you can do a body scan to identify where your emotion lives. It's a pretty simple technique. The way I do it, I pretend there's a futuristic laser body scanner, a red laser going horizontally from the top of my head all the way down to the bottom of my toes.
That helps me focus on one area at a time. As it moves, I can ask myself whether what I'm feeling lives there, and notice anything else that comes up.
This could be something very organized, like yoga, or maybe tai chi. Practices like these can really build your awareness of what's happening in your body, as well as your emotions.

But you can also do simpler things. I don't expect you to go do yoga in this moment to be mindful. Maybe that's not practical. Something like fidgeting might be. If you can fidget with an object, you can pay attention to what it's like to fidget. I like to fidget with my AirPods case. I roll it around in my palm. I like the smoothness, the way the plastic feels. It's a small movement, but it's possible to be mindful of what it's like.
I think breath is a really good way to be mindful and connected to yourself. Your breath is always there. It's always present. For the most part it's predictable. There's a rhythm to it.

Find a quiet, comfortable place to sit or lie down if you can. Close your eyes if you want to. You don't have to. Then bring your attention, as best you can, to your breath. Notice the sensations of breathing in and breathing out, without trying to control it. Let your body breathe the way it already knows how to. You get to be a curious observer, witnessing the process of breathing.

The only breathing technique I like to recommend is to extend your exhale. Doing so activates the parasympathetic system, which helps keep that safety state active a little longer as you breathe out. When you breathe in, the sympathetic system actually comes on just a little bit.
Writing, or other kinds of creativity like art, painting, or drawing, can be a great way to allow and process your emotions and to develop mindfulness.

If you're going to do this, focus on what's happening right here and right now, not the past exactly. I don't encourage people to retell trauma narratives in their journaling unless they really know they can handle it. That's something else. In general I don't recommend it, especially if you're new to this. To me, journaling is best for what's happening in this moment. What am I thinking? What am I feeling? You can be extremely literal about what's happening right here, right now.
Three of my favorite journaling tips:

ol: Match your writing speed to what you feel inside. It's okay to feel anxious in the present moment, of course. If you feel your body starting to rev up, your heartbeat picking up, a little jittery inside, then write faster. Let it come out. Use your hand and arm as an avenue for that energy to come out, with your pen or pencil as an extension of you.

Focus on the process, not the outcome. Don't worry about people reading it. That's not what it's about. Don't worry about it looking pretty, or about it being a final product. It's a journey in the moment of feeling what you're feeling, without an outcome in mind of what it should be once you're done.

Don't use a journal. You don't have to write in a journal. You can type, write, draw, sketch, or doodle. You can use a chalkboard if you like. It doesn't matter. Don't restrict yourself to how this should be. Pick what feels best for you and is most accessible, and use that.

blocks.why: This article talks about mindfulness. This practice gives you a few minutes of it.
